#138423. Breaking: Gigabyte MO27Q2A 27-inch QHD 280 Hz QD-OLED gaming monitor review: Another price buster from Gigabyte

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2331 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Gigabyte MO27Q2A 27-inch QHD 280 Hz QD-OLED gaming monitor review: Another price buster from Gigabyte

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2331 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Gigabyte MO27Q2A is a superlative value among 27-inch QHD OLEDs with high performance, accurate color and premium build quality.
  • Excellent build quality with mostly metal construction.
  • Industry observers note that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Gigabyte MO27Q2A is a superlative value among 27-inch QHD OLEDs with high performance, accurate color and premium build quality. It matches or exceeds many more expensive monitors.

Bright, sharp, and colorful picture.

Pro-level accuracy out of the box.

Useful Adobe RGB and sRGB color modes.

Tactical Switch for quick resolution changes.

Excellent build quality with mostly metal construction.

Industry observers note that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

I have long noted that choices are important, and nowhere is that better illustrated than in the best OLED gaming monitor category. Once an exotic and expensive technology, it is now much more affordable, thanks to a plethora of new models coming to market.

It has been revealed that gigabyte is certainly a leader in the price war with new models that deliver tremendous performance, image quality, and value. Its latest effort is a 27-inch QHD OLED model that refreshes at 280 Hz. It’s the MO27Q2A, and it leaves nothing out in its quest to be fast, beautiful, and packed with features. You get Adaptive-Sync with G-Sync and FreeSync certification, wide gamut color courtesy of Quantum Dot tech, HDR10, VESA DisplayHDR 400 True Black, USB ports with KVM, internal speakers and a better-than-average stand. Let’s take a look.

Quantum Dot Organic Light Emitting Diode (QD-OLED).

Max Resolution and Refresh Rate.

VESA DisplayHDR 400 True Black, HDR10.

It has been revealed that if there’s one thing that the MO27Q2A leaves out, it's LED lighting. There’s no colorful show to dazzle your opponents with. But nothing else has been sacrificed. There are HDMI 2.1 ports, DisplayPort 1.4 with DSC (Display Stream Compression), USB-C that supports video and 18 watts of power, plus USB Type-A and Type-B ports with KVM control. A pair of five-watt internal speakers delivers good audio, or you can use the 3.5mm headphone jack.

The screen is super colorful with over 108% coverage of DCI-P3 thanks to a Quantum Dot layer. Color is very accurate, so much so that I found calibration completely unnecessary. You get sRGB and Adobe RGB options as well. Brightness is solid at 250 nits for a full field and over 1,000 nits for a 3% window pattern. You can use variable brightness for SDR and HDR content to pump up small highlights for even more dynamic range.

In a recent development, high-performance gaming is the primary goal here, and for that, the MO27Q2A comes with a reliable 280 Hz refresh rate, Adaptive-Sync with certifications from Nvidia and AMD, and a host of Game Assist features like aiming points, sniper modes, flash suppression, timers, and a frame counter. Like all OLEDs, it has lightning-fast reflexes with super smooth motion rendering.

Gigabyte pays plenty of attention to panel care with a host of options like pixel refresh and logo detection. There’s extensive passive cooling (no fans) and AI control that tracks usage at the pixel level to keep everything in balance. The end result is longevity and reliability, which is backed by a three-year factory warranty that includes burn-in.

The MO27Q2A’s value is the most impressive part. At this writing, it sells for $399 online. It wasn’t long ago that you’d pay that for a 240 Hz QHD LCD. That category has dropped in cost as well, with some screens coming in around $200. But spending an extra $200 for an OLED seems like a no-brainer to me. Let’s see how the MO27Q2A fares in my tests.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Sources indicate that gigabyte offers a bit of fanfare on the MO27Q2A’s carton with colored graphics that set it apart from the plain brown wrappers more commonly seen at the big box store. A clamshell lid opens to reveal blocks of crumbly foam containing the panel, upright, and base, which assemble without tools. The power supply is internal, so you get a selection of IEC cords plus cables for HDMI, DisplayPort, and USB. A little clip goes on the stand to tidy up the wiring.

The panel is minimalist from the front with a thin flush bezel and a metal backing that wraps around the edges. A narrow trim strip crosses the bottom with a tiny Gigabyte logo in its center. The controls are under the center point and consist of a backlit joystick and two keys. One is the Tactical Switch, and it changes resolutions on the fly. More about that below.

Sources indicate that the stand is above average in quality with all-metal construction and smooth ergonomics. It includes 5.2 inches of height range plus 5/21 degrees tilt, 15 degrees swivel, and a 90-degree portrait mode. There is no hint of wobble or play. It is one of the better stands I’ve encountered, and I’ve encountered many.

From the side, you can see the panel-on-bulge design that is shared by many OLEDs. Not only does this look cool, but it actually is cool. The MO27Q2A’s panel is backed by metal, which acts as a heat sink. The bulge is also well ventilated, enough so that no fans are needed. A graphene layer behind the OLED contributes to cooling and hence, longevity.

Recent findings suggest that underneath is a well-appointed I/O panel with two HDMI 2.1s, a DisplayPort 1.4 with DSC, a USB-C that supports video and 18 watts of power, and USB 3.2, one upstream and two down. They can be bound to different video inputs using the KVM feature in the OSD. You also get a 3.5mm headphone jack and a pair of internal speakers with five watts of amplification.

The MO27Q2A’s OSD presents complete information with signal status at the top and current settings shown at the bottom.

Sources indicate that the Gaming menu includes a black frame insertion feature called Ultra Clear. It works at 280 or 120 Hz and is effective at removing motion blur. If you can run at 180fps or higher, you won’t need it. Other options include Black Equalizer, which increases shadow visibility, super resolution (edge enhancement, do not use), display mode for aspect ratio control, and a VRR toggle.

The MO27Q2A includes 10 picture modes mainly aimed at different game types. It comes out of the box in Eco, which limits brightness. Choose Standard to unlock the maximum light output. Within this mode, you can adjust color temp and gamma and choose a color space. My sample was nearly perfect out of the box, so good, in fact, that I could not improve it with calibration. If you want sRGB or Adobe RGB color, those choices are in the Color Space submenu. For sRGB, there’s an sRGB picture mode. HDR signals get their own five modes. Peak 1000 is the brightest and best choice there.

Industry observers note that you can use the KVM Wizard to bind USB ports and video inputs. That way, one keyboard, mouse, and monitor can service multiple sources like a PC and a gaming console, for instance. You can also view two sources at once using the PIP/PBP options.

In a recent development, quick Switch lets the user program the functions of the joystick directionals. It provides quick access to commonly used functions like brightness or crosshairs.

It has been revealed that A separate screen comes up for the MO27Q2A’s OLED care options. This is where you’ll find APL Stabilize, which has two levels of variable brightness or a constant setting. Its terminology is counterintuitive because Low means off, while Middle and High modulate light output more aggressively. High has the most dynamic range, with 1,000 peaks possible in HDR mode. If it were up to me, APL Stabilize would be in the Picture menu and be called Variable Brightness. Additional care options include pixel orbiting, panel refresh, and dimming for logos and corners. You turn any or all of these off if you wish.

Press the joystick and click right for the Game Assist menu and its plethora of play aids. You get four crosshairs, a timer, stopwatch, refresh rate indicator, and positioning of the information window. Also included are sniper mode and night vision. Flash Dimming suppresses your weapon’s muzzle flash if that becomes a distraction.

Sources indicate that gigabyte’s Tactical Switch is a unique feature that switches the MO27Q2A’s resolution on the fly. You can have FHD or HD in 16:9, 4:3, or 5:4 aspect ratios. The refresh rate remains at 280 Hz, but by shrinking the image, you get higher frame rates with no significant sharpness penalty.

Recent findings suggest that there isn’t much to the MO27Q2A’s calibration because it isn’t necessary. In fact, I could not improve my sample with calibration. It measures nearly perfect out of the box for D65, 2.2 gamma, and coverage of DCI-P3. The sRGB mode, which is also very accurate, is found in the picture mode list. For Adobe RGB, go to the Color Space sub-menu. For gaming and daily use, I settled on Standard mode, Native color space, and left everything else at default settings. My recommendations are below.

It has been revealed that for HDR signals, HDR is the default mode, but I found the same excellent accuracy and high brightness in the Peak 1000 mode. It delivers the promised 1,000 nits for a 3% window, which in my tests equated to 445 nits for a 25% window pattern. You get a number of sliders for brightness and contrast, but they are not needed unless you want a different look for HDR content.

A great way to evaluate a monitor’s HDR accuracy is by viewing static content that covers the full dynamic range of both color and neutral tones. Doom Eternal has such a screen in its HDR adjustment menu, and I use it for every review to verify detail rendering. The MO27Q2A revealed every nuance in this torture test, which told me that it is very color accurate and tracks luminance correctly. In simple terms, you’ll see everything the game creators put in.

This gives gameplay a heightened sense of realism, especially in textures like stone, metal, and dirt. The MO27Q2A let me almost reach out and touch them. I had to remind myself that its resolution was QHD and Ultra HD because it rendered so finely. I also saw rich color that was perfectly balanced. You’ll see in the SDR and HDR tests that this is a seriously precise monitor.

Gameplay was up to the premium OLED standard with smooth motion that was completely free of blur. I had no trouble maintaining a constant 280fps. If you can’t hit that speed, Gigabyte includes Ultra Clear, which is a black frame insertion feature. It will remove motion blur at lower rates like 120 Hz. I noted that it was available at 280 Hz as well, which is unusual. It cuts brightness by around 40%, but you can partially compensate for that with the brightness slider. It operated artifact-free.

Another way to increase frame rates is with the Tactical Switch, which changes resolution and picture size on the fly. It doesn’t increase the refresh rate, but by shrinking the image, it maintains a favorable pixel map so that sharpness doesn’t take a huge hit.

Gameplay was addictive during my numerous frag fests. Input lag and response are super quick, which helped make my aim more precise. The MO27Q2A was so fast that it made me overconfident. I rushed into the melee rather than picking off enemies one by one. It was truly difficult to stop playing.

The MO27Q2A excels as an everyday screen with 109ppi pixel density in its 27-inch form factor. It’s significantly less expensive than an Ultra HD monitor if you can accept a small reduction in clarity. And that resolution is a sweet spot for frame rates. You won’t need a giga-hauler video card to achieve its full potential.

Accurate color out of the box meant I could rely on the MO27Q2A as a reference for graphics and photos. I found excellent results in my initial tests, and I could not improve upon them with adjustments. This monitor is pro-level for sure.

It’s impressive ergonomically too, with a solid all-metal stand and rugged panel construction. There are no missing features except for flashy LEDs. The internal speakers play loud and clear in the upper midrange, or you can plug in headphones. Users with a PC and console will appreciate the USB ports and KVM functions.

Recent findings suggest that takeaway: The MO27Q2A is a truly full-featured gaming monitor that can double as an everyday screen or a professional display. It games on par with the very best screens I’ve reviewed and delivers performance equal to more expensive OLEDs with higher refresh rates. It also matches those products in build quality with a solid stand and metal construction. For $399, you’ll be hard-pressed to find better.

Grand Theft Auto VI understands just how important a smartphone is

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Text messages, social networking, selfies — the device is integrated into every aspect of your virtual life.
  • Text messages, social networking, selfies — the device is integrated into every aspect of your virtual life.
  • Grand Theft Auto VI, in many ways, tries to simulate real life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Text messages, social networking, selfies — the device is integrated into every aspect of your virtual life.

Text messages, social networking, selfies — the device is integrated into every aspect of your virtual life.

Grand Theft Auto VI, in many ways, tries to simulate real life. And life in 2026 would not be complete without a smartphone. GTA VI understands this and makes the phone not just a central part of the experience, but an object that exists within the world. You may try to escape into a fantasy of robbing banks and fighting drug lords, but you can’t get away from texts from your mom or nagging fitness app notifications.

Industry observers note that seeing a smartphone in a game isn’t a new phenomenon. The device has become a natural stand-in for the main menu in many games, giving players an interface that feels intuitive, because a phone is something they use every day. But the phone in GTA VI is different for a few reasons. One is that it behaves much like any other object in the game, whether it’s a gun or a bottle of beer. The action doesn’t pause when you use your phone. Instead, the game switches to a first-person viewpoint, where you can still walk around — or drive, if you’re feeling ambitious — while reading texts or flipping through a fictional version of Instagram.

Rob Nelson, the co-studio head at developer Rockstar North and producer on GTA VI, indicates that it would’ve felt “archaic” to have a static phone that worked like those in other games, or the one in GTA V, which appeared as a pop-up at the bottom of the screen across from the minimap. “We felt that it was important to make it physical so you have to look at it and put your attention on it, including while driving,” he explains. “It’s about finding the line between realism and player convenience. But the act of being lost in your phone felt like something worth doing, even though it could mean slightly more inconvenience. In this game you are committing to using it.” (Of course, texting and driving, like much of what you do in GTA VI, is both very dangerous and very illegal.).

You have to interact with the phone in the game constantly. Often the story plays out through phone calls and text messages, and you have a surprisingly large array of apps to use that serve a real purpose in the game. You manage your money in a banking app, use a rideshare app when you need a lift, track your workouts in a fitness app, scroll through a social network complete with comments and the ability to like posts, and sideload an AI tool that scans nearby cars so you can see how easy they’ll be to steal. You can even change the wallpaper and ringtone. (GTA VI has two main characters that you swap between, and each has their own phone, though they’re functionally identical.).

Industry observers note that what’s most impressive is how all of these apps interact with each other. For instance, after pulling off a major heist, a friend might text you a news story about it, asking “was this you!?” You can then click the link, open up the news app, and read an actual article about what went down. These kinds of interactions can be functional, like when another character texts you a location, which you can then add to your map so the GPS can guide you there. Other times, they add texture to the world or depth to the characters. GTA VI is a love story about two criminals named Jason and Lucia, and you play as both. At one point, while controlling Lucia, I got a text asking for a selfie. I opened up the camera, shot a pic of Lucia drinking a latte, and sent it over. Jason replied immediately — and their relationship got a boost.

Industry observers note that phones are so fully integrated into the game that they can even interrupt the characters’ sleep. At the end of each day, you can click on a bed to rest for the night. But neither Jason nor Lucia will instantly fall asleep when you do — instead, they’ll sit down and pull out their phone, and you have the option to doomscroll or catch up on texts instead of going to sleep right away. Nelson says that this was implemented because the developers wanted to include the ability for the characters to sit on the bed at night, much like a real couple in a shared living space might do. “We needed something to do aside from just sitting there staring at nothing,” he says.

If nothing else, GTA VI’s phone shows how alike we all are: Even bank robbers being hunted by the police can’t seem to stop scrolling. “Phones are a constant part of our lives,” Nelson states of the evolution, “even more than they were in 2013.”.

Sources indicate that adding real-time video to a web app used to mean plugins, proprietary SDKs and a lot of money. Today every modern browser ships with WebRTC, a set of APIs that lets two browsers exchange audio, video and data directly. The catch is that WebRTC gives you building blocks, not a finished feature. This guide walks through those blocks in the order you actually need them, with the exact API calls you need, and then covers the production issues that tutorials usually skip.

A browser-to-browser call has four moving parts:.

Sources indicate that start with the local preview. Browsers only allow camera access on HTTPS or localhost, so serve your page accordingly.

Sources indicate that 1. Request a stream with navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia(), passing video constraints (an ideal width of 1280 and height of 720 is a sensible default) and audio constraints with echoCancellation and noiseSuppression enabled.

2. Assign the returned MediaStream to the srcObject property of your local video element.

According to recent reports, 3. Keep a reference to the stream, because you will add its tracks to the peer connection later.

Industry observers note that set the muted and playsinline attributes on the local video element. Without muted consumers hear themselves, and without playsinline iOS Safari opens the video full screen.

The peers need a way to find each other. A tiny Node.js server using the ws package is enough for development. Its whole job is to relay messages between the peers in a room:.

In a recent development, 1. Create a WebSocket server (for example with the ws package) listening on its own port.

2. Keep a map of room names to the set of sockets in each room.

Recent findings suggest that 3. When a client sends a join message, store the room name on the socket and add it to that room's set.

4. For every other message type, forward the raw message to the other sockets in the same room, and never echo it back to the sender.

5. On disconnect, remove the socket from its room so stale peers do not receive messages.

In production you would add authentication, limit room size to two for one-to-one calls, and validate message types, but the shape stays the same.

Both sides create an RTCPeerConnection, add their local tracks and listen for the remote ones:.

Industry observers note that 1. Create a new RTCPeerConnection with an iceServers list that contains at least one STUN server.

It has been revealed that 2. Loop over the local stream's tracks and call addTrack() for each one.

In a recent development, 3. In the ontrack handler, attach the first remote stream to your remote video element.

4. In the onicecandidate handler, send every new candidate to the other peer through your signalling channel as a candidate message.

According to recent reports, one peer creates an offer, the other answers, and both apply each other's descriptions. Candidates arrive asynchronously in the background.

1. The caller runs createOffer(), applies it with setLocalDescription() and sends the description as an offer message.

Recent findings suggest that 2. The callee applies the offer with setRemoteDescription(), runs createAnswer(), applies it locally and sends it back as an answer.

It has been revealed that 3. The caller applies the answer with setRemoteDescription().

4. Both sides pass every incoming candidate message to addIceCandidate().

Industry observers note that if both peers might start a call at the same time, look up the "perfect negotiation" pattern on MDN. It assigns one side as polite and resolves offer collisions cleanly instead of leaving both peers stuck.

Sources indicate that on a home network, STUN alone often works. On corporate Wi-Fi, mobile carriers and symmetric NATs it frequently does not, and the call silently fails to connect. A TURN server relays media when a direct path is impossible. The open-source coturn server is the usual choice.

In practice, your iceServers list should contain your own STUN URL plus a TURN URL with a username and credential, so the browser can fall back to the relay automatically when direct connectivity fails.

Generate short-lived TURN credentials on your backend rather than hard-coding them, and budget for bandwidth: relayed calls pass every frame through your server.

Industry observers note that owners deny camera access, unplug headsets and switch from Wi-Fi to 4G mid-call. Catch NotAllowedError and show a clear explanation, listen for devicechange events, and use RTCRtpSender.replaceTrack() to swap cameras without renegotiating the whole call.

Industry observers note that listen to pc.onconnectionstatechange. When the state becomes disconnected, wait a few seconds before giving up, because it often recovers. On failed, call pc.restartIce() to try fresh network paths.

Use RTCRtpSender.setParameters() to cap the bitrate on weak connections, and read pc.getStats() to monitor packet loss and round-trip time. Showing a small "poor connection" indicator does more for perceived quality than any codec tweak.

It has been revealed that mesh calls, where every participant connects to every other, work for two or three people. Beyond that, upload bandwidth explodes. Group calls need a Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU) such as mediasoup, LiveKit or Janus, which receives each stream once and forwards it to the others.

Recent findings suggest that tutorials end at a working demo, but the fastest way to understand what production WebRTC looks like is to watch a real call from the inside. Chrome ships an internal diagnostics page that demonstrates every peer connection the browser opens, and it works on any site that uses WebRTC.

According to recent reports, 1. Open chrome://webrtc-internals in one tab and keep it open.

It has been revealed that 2. In another tab, start a call on your own demo and find its RTCPeerConnection entry.

3. Expand that entry and look at the ICE candidate pairs: you will see whether the call went direct (host or srflx) or through a TURN relay (relay).

According to recent reports, 4. Open the stats graphs for the outbound video stream and watch the bitrate, frame rate and resolution adapt when you throttle the network in DevTools.

5. Check the negotiated codec and how rapidly the connection recovers when you switch Wi-Fi off and back on.

Once you can read your own call, repeat the exercise on a production service. Any browser-based product works, whether a meeting tool or a live video chat that pairs two visitors, because webrtc-internals shows the same data for every site. Expect differences from your demo: more candidate pairs, a relay candidate in the list and a bitrate that adapts faster. Seeing them makes the earlier sections concrete, from why TURN matters to how bandwidth estimation reacts to packet loss.

The one-to-one call above is the core of many products, from telehealth consultations and tutoring to customer support. The engineering challenges grow with the use case: random matching needs queueing and presence on the signalling server, public platforms need moderation and reporting, and global audiences need TURN servers in several regions.

Sources indicate that start with the minimal version, get it working across Chrome, Firefox and Safari on both desktop and mobile, and add TURN before real users arrive. Once the call is reliable, every other feature becomes a much easier problem.

  • Recent findings suggest that the above Tweet indicates you the SNES app splash screen, chat window, and an animation of someone interacting with chat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that nintendo’s classic SNES console now has its own ChatGPT chatbot. Due to the platform's age and limited resources, things are kept in check, though. For example, the (small) language model is a 2.2-million-parameter distillation of OpenAI’s GPT-OSS-120b. Nevertheless, Vintage Computing blogger Benj Edwards has attempted to squeeze the best performance from this incongruous tech combo by accelerating the chatbot's responsiveness using “the Super NES's best GPU, the Super FX 2 chip.”.

AI runs on GPUs, so I wondered: how good would @ChatGPT be if it ran on the Super NES's best GPU, the Super FX 2 chip? With the help of GPT-6 Astra and gpt-oss, I present unofficial ChatGPT for SNES: 2.2M parameters on a real Super Nintendo. It can make mistakes, but it's fun https://t.co/TAJ4jYREo7November 19, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the above Tweet indicates you the SNES app splash screen, chat window, and an animation of someone interacting with chat. If that’s tempting you to give ChatGPT for SNES a test run, there are several options. Easiest first, you can head on over to this page where Edwards has embedded the SNES9x emulator, which can load the app. Once there, choose the 4MB model, or a 19MB one with the opening sentences of 150,000 Simple English Wikipedia articles integrated into the knowledge base (stored in the cartridge's MSU-1 data file). We recommend the latter, so the model knows a few more facts and can work as a calculator.

When you load it, the SNES app asks you to press Start. If you are sat at your PC keyboard, just hit Enter. You don’t need a joypad for text entry either, thankfully; just get typing to interact with ChatGPT for SNES (as long as the window is in focus). While you’re interacting with this chatbot, you can enjoy SNES-appropriate input sound effects, plus a chirpy chip-tune soundtrack.

According to recent reports, in our tests, the usefulness of the ChatGPT for SNES app, beyond its curiosity value, was very limited. Edwards admits as much on the project's embedded interactive page, explaining that “the model is millions of times smaller than the models behind ChatGPT.” Naturally, with a small and fuzzy knowledge base, “You’ll get some fun and weird stuff,” says the Vintage Computing blogger.

Using Nintendo Super FX 2 technology to accelerate the language model is a masterstroke for the project. This coprocessor chip enhanced SNES games with faster 2D and 3D graphics and debuted with Yoshi's Island. Inside the SFX2, which had to be manufacturer-installed on any game cartridge that required it, was a 21.47 MHz RISC CPU. Contrast that to the SNES main CPU, a 16-bit Ricoh 5A22 running at 2.68 MHz.

Nintendo's second version of the SFX retained the polygon and advanced 2D effect capabilities of the original but ran at full speed internally (rather than half speed) and supported larger ROM sizes. Like Yoshi’s Island, it would be integrated into the Doom cartridge.

Sources indicate that edwards’ ChatGPT for SNES isn’t just an online diversion. It can also be downloaded and run/played on a real vintage SNES. You’ll also need a flash cart for the console with Super FX support, and MSU-1 support if you prefer the build including the abridged Wikipedia fact book.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Given how good the game is on console, the wait will almost certainly be worth it.

Given how good the game is on console, the wait will almost certainly be worth it.

Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here for millions of players who own a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X / S, and those who strategy to buy a console, despite rising costs this year, just to play it. As you have likely already noticed, the launch is inescapable, and that’s especially tough if you’re a PC gamer.

According to recent reports, I’m sorry to remind you that the clock has only just now started ticking down to the unannounced yet inevitable release of the PC version. Good luck with avoiding Twitch and browsing the internet while trying to remain oblivious to the violent (and romantic) delights that await you.

Seeing Leonida in true 4K at an unlocked frame rate with full ray-tracing effects and extended draw distances, among other graphical improvements, might be a thing you can do on your PC as early as sometime in Q1 2027, if recent reports are accurate. Regardless, early 2027 is not right now. Speaking as someone with a capable gaming desktop, I’m sad to say that FOMO has already gotten the best of me. I bought GTA VI on the PS5 and will probably double-dip and buy it again on PC, just like I did with GTA V and Red Dead Redemption 2. The psychology of me, a weak-willed consumer, is one that publisher Rockstar Games and really any other company in its position would be happy to exploit.

According to recent reports, the PC version of GTA VI will launch, eventually, in a very different landscape than the PC ports of Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA V did. Despite the recent downturn in PC sales driven by increased RAM prices, there are considerably more players on PC now than there were a decade ago. SteamDB’s charts show that Steam’s concurrent consumers alone have more than doubled (from around 20 million to over 40 million now) since 2020.

Recent findings suggest that A chunk of those people are likely made up of console expats who decided to migrate to PC for various reasons. Some wanted to experience the fun of building their own desktop, while some were mainly convinced by the fact that you can get more power for your money with a PC than with a PlayStation 5 Pro or Xbox Series X. For a subset of people, the convenience of getting something like a Steam Deck to bring your PC game library with you anywhere more than makes up for its lack of power. There are many other justifiable reasons for making PC your main gaming platform, like getting faster access to discounts on digital games, not paying for online multiplayer, ultrawide monitor resolutions, being able to buy games from one of several platforms, and having one device that you can use for work and play.

Rockstar seems poised to deliver the definitive version of GTA VI on PC on its own terms, and I’m interested to see what the end result will be. In addition to building the best-looking version of the game made to run well across countless configurations, its PC optimization efforts are likely also more focused than before on ensuring decent performance on lower-end hardware (including PC handhelds). With a 200-plus-gigabyte install size on consoles, I dread how major it’ll be on PC.

Ideally, the PC version will launch alongside an improved version of GTA Online (whether it’s free to play is anyone’s guess), and maybe with upgraded GTA roleplay tech to support it. I’m hopeful that the PC version of GTA VI will come in early 2027, but if the numerous delays of the console versions were any indication, the developer will take all the time it needs to get it right.

Upgrade, 9:55AM ET, November 19th: The SteamDB data cited now specifies that it’s concurrent people, not the number of users total.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The console’s latest patch finally activates its dormant Wi-Fi hardware, enabling a handful of new features.

The console’s latest update finally activates its dormant Wi-Fi hardware, enabling a handful of new features.

Analogue has long been good at expanding the features and functionality of its consoles through regular firmware updates, but installing those updates has always required moving files around with a memory card. That’s no longer the case with the Analogue 3D, the organization’s modernized version of the Nintendo 64. Although the console has had Wi-Fi hardware since day one, it’s only now been finally activated through the last enhancement you’ll need to install with a memory card.

According to recent reports, analogue on Wednesday released the version 1.6.0 firmware for the Analogue 3D, adding support for 2.4GHz, 5GHz, mixed, and hidden Wi-Fi networks. Once the patch is installed, the Wi-Fi setup process will begin automatically when the console is booted, but there’s now an added Wi-Fi section in the Analogue 3D’s settings menu for updating passwords and other details later.

Industry observers note that the console’s newly introduced Wi-Fi capabilities add a couple of useful features at launch. In the future, the Analogue 3D will be able to download and install firmware updates so it automatically keeps itself up to date. The new wireless capabilities enable automatic date and time settings based on your time zone, too, and in the privacy section of the console’s settings menu, you’ll now find an option for sharing “anonymous usage and analytics data” with Analogue to help further improve its hardware.

#138412. Rapidus reportedly struggles to produce working SRAM on its 2nm node, putting 2027 mass production at risk

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1473 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Rapidus reportedly struggles to produce working SRAM on its 2nm node, putting 2027 mass production at risk

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1473 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, rapidus is reportedly facing challenges in developing functioning SRAM cells using its 2nm-class node, which relies on EUV lithography.
  • It has been revealed that bloomberg's report spells bad news for the Japanese firm.
  • "Then we had a testing and July 10th we confirmed a major milestone: we successfully obtained electrical characteristics of 2-nanometer node GAA transistors," remarked Atsuyoshi Koikem, chief executive of Rapidus, at Hot Chips 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, rapidus is reportedly facing challenges in developing functioning SRAM cells using its 2nm-class node, which relies on EUV lithography. According to a fresh report, Rapidus has missed a critical milestone to demonstrate working SRAM cells this summer, despite the Japanese company's efforts in producing semiconductor test structures at its fab in Japan in mid-2025. In addition, the company is allegedly fighting contamination in its cleanroom. This puts the prepares of the government-backed startup to begin mass production of chips in 2027 at risk.

It has been revealed that bloomberg's report spells bad news for the Japanese firm. Rapidus began to produce test structures with 2nm-class Gate-All-Around (GAA) transistors at its IIM-1 facility in Hokkaido in July 2025, nearly 16 months ago. At the time, the company announced that its prototype transistors exhibited the expected electrical characteristics, which suggested that its equipment and fundamental process steps worked as intended.

"Then we had a testing and July 10th we confirmed a major milestone: we successfully obtained electrical characteristics of 2-nanometer node GAA transistors," remarked Atsuyoshi Koikem, chief executive of Rapidus, at Hot Chips 2025. "We can see the transistor actually works.".

Sources indicate that however, production of individual transistors is considerably easier than fabrication of functional integrated circuits (ICs) with multiple interconnected devices. According to sources at Bloomberg, Rapidus was supposed to demonstrate functional static random-access memory (SRAM) cells by summer 2026, but has yet to achieve this milestone. It is noteworthy that the report does not reveal whether Rapidus is struggling with individual SRAM cells, larger memory arrays, or achieving acceptable electrical characteristics and yields, so we will have to speculate.

Sources indicate that SRAM is fundamental to modern processors because it serves as cache memory and forms other on-chip memory structures, which can contain hundreds of millions of bitcells. Furthermore, SRAM arrays are vital vehicles for early process evaluation, as their repetitive structures expose manufacturing defects, transistor variability, and other problems that may not become apparent during tests of individual transistors.

A conventional 6T SRAM bitcell consists of six transistors: two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) and two access transistors. However, these transistors also require contacts and local interconnects, as well as connections to wordlines, bitlines, and power rails (VDD and VSS). Meanwhile, a complete SRAM macro also requires peripheral circuits, such as row decoders, sense amplifiers, write drivers, and control logic, which makes a 256 KB SRAM macro quite a sophisticated IC. As a result, chipmakers usually use both SRAM cell arrays and SRAM macros as primary means to evaluate, monitor, and qualify process technologies at various stages. Furthermore, low defect density of SRAM macros is crucial for good yields of SRAM-intensive chip designs.

Sources indicate that the importance of SRAM makes Rapidus' reported difficulties particularly concerning given its intention to begin commercial production in 2027. While the firm does not confirm delays in mass production using its 2nm fabrication technology, in an interview with the Japan Times, representatives at Rapidus already mentioned that the company was on track to mass-produce chips in the second half of fiscal 2027, which ends on March 31, 2028. Previously, Rapidus had specified its production targets without specifying calendar years or fiscal years, which by default implied the calendar year.

Before it can mass-produce processors for customers, the firm must demonstrate functional SRAM cells, integrate them into larger arrays, achieve acceptable yields, qualify its process technology, and then initiate risk production around a year before the start of high-volume manufacturing (HVM).

It has been revealed that chipmakers do not generally disclose detailed schedules for SRAM development and milestones as far as new manufacturing technologies are concerned. However, TSMC tends to share progress on its upcoming nodes using the performance and yield of a 256 Mb SRAM array or '256 Mb SRAM yield on an internal product-like vehicle.' For example, TSMC's N2 demonstrated more than 80% of its target device performance and over 50% yield on a 256Mb SRAM test chip in April 2023. By April 2024, the process had advanced to more than 90% of its target device performance and over 80% SRAM yield. About half a year before mass production started, in May 2025, N2 transistor performance was close to 100%, whereas 256 Mb SRAM average yield was over 90%. By contrast, Rapidus has not declared any SRAM progress so far, and Bloomberg reports that the manufacturer has failed to produce functioning static random access memory cells, meaning that its SRAM yield is 0%.

While there is no rule of thumb that a firm must have a functional SRAM array or macro N quarters before mass production of chips with that array or macro, it is evident that the reported setback leaves Rapidus with limited time to complete its crucial development milestones before kicking off mass production by the end of fiscal 2027.

Production of 2nm-class chips with GAA transistors and extreme ultraviolet lithography is exceptionally complicated, even for established chipmakers. So far, only Intel, TSMC, and Samsung have begun mass production of chips using nodes that rely on GAA devices. Unlike FinFETs, GAA transistors feature multiple vertically stacked silicon nanosheets surrounded by gate materials, which improves electrostatic control but introduces additional fabrication challenges. Furthermore, extremely small feature dimensions require exceptional precision in deposition, etching, lithography, and process control. For Rapidus, which was founded only in 2022 and relies on process technology IP developed by IBM, the task of reproducing these processes consistently in a new fab represents an incredibly tall task.

One potential problem involves selective removal of silicon-germanium (SiGe) layers that separate silicon nanosheets during fabrication. These sacrificial layers must be removed without damage to the silicon channels or significant changes to their dimensions. Insufficient etching can leave unwanted material between nanosheets, whereas excessive etching can reduce channel thickness or increase surface roughness. A research paper published by imec identifies nanosheet release as one of the critical challenges of GAA manufacturing, particularly because variations in channel geometry can affect transistor performance and consistency.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, EUV lithography itself introduces additional complications. At extremely small dimensions, stochastic effects associated with photon absorption, resist chemistry, and subsequent pattern transfer can produce variations in feature dimensions, edge roughness, and occasional missing or malformed structures. Such defects can affect pretty much everything, including transistor gates, contacts, and interconnects. In fact, there is a firm called Fractilia that specializes solely in stochastic controls. Although individual test transistors may function correctly, circuits with millions of interconnected devices are much more vulnerable to failures caused by stochastic defects.

Another potential challenge concerns inner spacer formation. These extremely small dielectric structures electrically isolate the gate from the source and drain regions. Their fabrication requires precise lateral etching of SiGe followed by dielectric deposition. Variations in spacer geometry can affect effective gate length, parasitic capacitance, leakage current, and transistor performance. A paper published in Nanomaterials in January 2026 demonstrates that even subtle differences in etching conditions can affect spacer geometry and nanosheet integrity, which potentially introduces electrical variability that becomes particularly problematic in SRAM circuits.

Industry observers note that gate stack integration presents another possible source of difficulties. GAA fabrication requires conformal deposition of gate dielectrics and metal materials around multiple nanosheets, including narrow spaces between them. Variations in material thickness, interfaces, and effective metal work function can alter transistor threshold voltages, which is not a major problem for individual transistors or tiny test patterns. However, for SRAM structures, excessive differences between nominally identical transistors can reduce read, write, and retention margins, which could prevent cells from operating reliably at their intended voltages and greatly narrow the manufacturing process window.

Sources indicate that finally, contact resistance, interconnect defects, and particle contamination can further complicate circuit integration. Bloomberg specifically reports that Rapidus is working to improve dust and particle control in its cleanroom. Normally, there might be no connection between contamination and the SRAM woes the company is experiencing. However, one of the distinct features of IIM-1 is that it uses an unconventional grid-based wafer transportation system to enable its single-batch processing as well as increase the efficiency of expedited processing. Usage of this system raises questions about whether the fresh infrastructure has undergone sufficient contamination and reliability qualification, though, again, a transportation system alone could not be responsible for zero (or near-zero) SRAM yield.

In a recent development, rapidus reportedly stresses that it remains committed to mass production in the second half of fiscal 2027. However, until the firm demonstrates functional SRAM and subsequently larger integrated circuits, questions about its ability to manufacture commercially viable 2nm chips will persist.

Recent findings suggest that anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

He was able to bring temperatures down from 84 degrees Celsius to 48.8 degrees Celsius, with Cyberpunk going from 47 FPS to 56 FPS.

Trash Bench was asked to review a laptop cooling stand, but he stated he doesn’t do reviews, so he proposed a video idea: He’ll test the laptop cooler and try to beat it with his creations—no opening the laptop, no sub-ambient cooling solutions, only airflow.

The Llano V12 laptop cooling fan sent to Trash Bench achieved an impressive 58.3 degrees Celsius average on the GPU at medium settings, dropping 27 degrees from the stock 84 degrees Celsius. The lower temperatures also improved gaming performance by an average of 19.4%. Pushing the Llano V12 to 100% made it incredibly loud, but it only reached 56.7 degrees Celsius with negligible performance gains.

His first attempt to beat the Llano V12 was using the Noctua NF-A20, a huge 200mm fan, and a 3D-printed duct with foam around the edges, like the Llano V12, to prevent air leaks. Unfortunately, the single 200mm fan didn't beat the Llano V12, with GPU temperatures averaging 66.3 degrees Celsius—still pretty impressive given the setup's simplicity, if you ignore the messy PC power supply and fan speed controller beside it.

It has been revealed that his second attempt used six Arctic P12 fans at full speed, beating the Llano V12 by 0.9 degrees Celsius at medium settings and achieving an average GPU temperature of 57.4 degrees Celsius. However, it lost to the full-speed Llano V12, but only barely. The third attempt used two 4000 RPM server fans, which were even louder than the six full-speed Arctic P12S — but that finally did the trick, beating the Llano V12 at 100% by 2.6 degrees Celsius.

And just to go extreme, like Trash Bench often does in his experiments, he used a powerful blower fan designed to inflate bounce houses. He took advantage of the larger foam gaskets the Llano V12 used and 3D-printed an interface at the bottom of the laptop cooler’s housing to fit a flexible duct. The sheer force of the air lifted the laptop off the stand, so it needed to be taped down to seal the air leak.

The bounce house blower produced an average GPU temperature of 48.8 degrees Celsius, but saw very little performance gain over the Llano V12 at 100%, six Arctic P12s, and the pair of server fans, with Time Spy benchmark results within 1% of each other. The Noctua was the weakest in the benchmarks, however, lagging by 3% behind the bounce house blower, but was much quieter.

Trash Bench admits that while lower temperatures are great, they reach diminishing returns once the thermal bottleneck disappears and another bottleneck takes over.

Valve announced some updates about Steam Machine availability today, including good news if you want to buy one right now and potential bad news about future supply due to RAMaggedon.

The good news: You can now purchase a 512GB Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist. Initially, interested buyers had to get on Valve’s waitlist if they wanted to purchase one, but the console-like PC is now available in an “add-to-cart” status, according to the company. As I write this, the 512GB versions with and without a bundled controller are showing estimated delivery dates of three to five business days on Valve’s website. The bad news: If you’re on the waitlist for a 2TB model, you might not get a chance to buy one at all, as Valve claims there are more people on the waitlist than there are units available. The company is closing the waitlists for its 2TB models.

Valve claims that while it’s still building more Steam machines, “memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels” and that it doesn’t know the number it can make or “at what price we’ll be able to offer them.” The 2TB Steam Machine is “especially constrained.” The manufacturer anticipates “having more information” to share about additional supply in January.

It has been revealed that after delaying the Steam Machine’s expected early 2026 launch due to the memory and storage crisis, Valve rolled out the product in June with a price starting at $1,049 for the 512GB model without a bundled controller. A 2TB model without a controller costs $1,349.

It has been revealed that email remains an key communication channel for web applications. From account verification and password resets to product announcements and customer notifications, many applications depend on email to keep consumers informed.

According to recent reports, for developers, however, implementing email functionality involves more than connecting a service and sending a message. A reliable email system needs to handle authentication, dynamic content, delivery failures, user preferences, event tracking, and integrations with other application components.

Industry observers note that using an email service provider (ESP) can simplify this process. Most modern providers offer REST APIs, SMTP relays, templates, automation features, and reporting tools that developers can integrate into existing applications.

This guide explores the technical considerations involved in building email integrations, including API-based sending, webhook handling, automation workflows, and deliverability.

There are two common ways to connect an application to an email delivery service: SMTP and REST APIs.

It has been revealed that SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is a standard protocol used to transfer email messages between servers. Developers can connect an application to an SMTP server using credentials and configuration settings.

REST APIs provide another approach. Instead of communicating through an email server protocol, an application sends HTTP requests to an endpoint. The provider processes the request and returns a response.

Both methods can support transactional and application-generated emails, but their implementation differs.

An application already supports SMTP configuration.

Developers want a relatively straightforward integration.

Existing frameworks or libraries provide built-in SMTP support.

An application needs programmatic control over email operations.

Developers want structured responses and error handling.

Email functionality needs to integrate with other application services.

The system requires event tracking or additional API capabilities.

The right approach depends on the application's architecture, expected email volume, and integration requirements.

An API integration allows an application to trigger emails in response to specific events.

For example, an ecommerce application might send an order confirmation after a successful payment. A SaaS application could send an account verification message after registration.

A typical integration follows this process:.

The application detects an event.

The backend prepares the recipient and message data.

The backend authenticates with the email provider.

The provider processes the request.

The application records the response and handles any errors.

Consider a Node.js application that needs to trigger an email campaign through an API.

Some platforms, including Mailmodo, provide REST API functionality for triggering campaigns and integrating external applications with email workflows.

The following example demonstrates the general structure of an HTTP request using a campaign-triggering endpoint:.

According to recent reports, this example uses the documented Mailmodo trigger endpoint and request structure. The campaign ID and API key must be replaced with the values from the relevant account.

Notice that the API key is loaded from an environment variable rather than written directly into the source code.

This is an important security practice. Credentials should never be exposed in frontend JavaScript, public repositories, or client-side application bundles.

Not every email provider offers the same integration capabilities. Developers should evaluate providers based on their API documentation, authentication methods, supported endpoints, event notifications, and integration flexibility.

For example, Elastic Email provides a REST API that developers can use to send emails and manage different email operations from an application.

According to recent reports, its API uses HTTPS requests and API-key authentication. Developers can use the available endpoints to send messages, manage campaigns, retrieve information, and configure webhook notifications.

When evaluating an email API, consider these technical requirements:.

Authentication: Check how API keys are generated, stored, restricted, and rotated.

Documentation: Look for clear endpoint descriptions, request examples, response formats, and error codes.

SDK availability: Official libraries can reduce the amount of integration code required.

Permission management: Separate credentials for sending emails and accessing account information can reduce unnecessary exposure.

API limitations: Review connection limits, request timeouts, rate limits, and account-level restrictions before deploying an integration.

Industry observers note that A provider with extensive features is not necessarily the best option for every project. The vital consideration is whether its API supports the application's actual requirements.

Sending an email is only one part of the communication process. Applications may also need to know what happens after a message is submitted.

This is where webhooks become useful.

A webhook allows an external service to send an HTTP notification to an application when a particular event occurs.

Depending on the provider, events may include:.

For example, an application could receive a delivery-failure notification and update the corresponding email record in its database.

A basic Express.js webhook endpoint might look like this:.

In a recent development, this is a simplified example rather than a complete provider-specific webhook implementation. A production endpoint should validate the provider's signature or other authentication mechanism and follow its documented payload structure.

Recent findings suggest that it should also handle duplicate events safely. Webhook providers may retry notifications when an application does not respond successfully.

An idempotent event handler prevents the same notification from creating duplicate database updates or triggering repeated actions.

Email automation connects application events with predefined communication sequences.

Instead of manually sending every message, developers can create workflows that respond to user activity.

Consider a SaaS application with the following registration process:.

The backend stores the new user.

A verification email is triggered.

If the user does not complete onboarding, a follow-up message may be triggered.

A simplified workflow can be represented as:.

In a production application, email delivery should generally be handled through a background job queue rather than blocking the registration request.

A queue also makes it easier to retry temporary failures, manage sending volume, and prevent email delays from affecting the main application.

Developers should consider tools such as Redis-backed queues or framework-specific job processors when building larger systems.

In a recent development, automation platforms can also help manage more complex journeys. For instance, a developer can connect application events to an external email workflow instead of implementing every communication sequence independently.

The key is to keep business logic in the application while using the email service to manage message delivery and relevant campaign operations.

A successful API response does not necessarily mean that an email has reached the recipient's inbox.

Email deliverability depends on several technical factors, including domain authentication, sender reputation, message quality, and recipient engagement.

Developers should pay attention to the following configurations.

Sender Policy Framework identifies the mail servers authorized to send messages on behalf of a domain.

A correctly configured SPF record helps receiving servers evaluate whether an email originates from an authorized source.

Industry observers note that domainKeys Identified Mail adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages. Receiving servers can use the corresponding public key in DNS to verify the signature.

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance builds on SPF and DKIM. It allows domain owners to publish policies for handling messages that fail authentication checks and receive reports about authentication activity.

These three mechanisms should be configured carefully, especially when an application sends emails through multiple providers.

It has been revealed that email systems generate useful operational data. However, developers should avoid treating every available metric as an accurate measure of user engagement.

For example, open tracking can be affected by privacy features and automated image loading. Click tracking may also include automated security scans.

More reliable application-level signals can include:.

These events can be connected with email campaign data to understand how communication affects application activity.

In a recent development, developers should also maintain a clear separation between email delivery records and user account records. This makes it easier to investigate delivery issues without unnecessarily modifying customer data.

When collecting engagement information, applications should follow applicable privacy requirements and respect user communication preferences.

Before deploying an email integration, developers should review the following areas:.

API security: Store credentials in environment variables or a dedicated secrets manager.

Domain authentication: Configure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.

Error handling: Account for failed requests, invalid recipients, and temporary provider errors.

Background processing: Use queues for asynchronous email delivery.

Webhook validation: Verify incoming notifications and handle duplicate events.

Monitoring: Track delivery failures, bounce rates, and application-level outcomes.

Testing: Test email templates across different clients and devices before production deployment.

These practices help create an email system that is easier to maintain, troubleshoot, and scale.

Email integration is an notable part of modern application development, but a reliable implementation requires more than connecting an SMTP server or calling an API endpoint.

Developers need to consider authentication, asynchronous processing, webhook security, automation logic, domain configuration, and event monitoring.

In a recent development, REST APIs are useful for applications that need programmatic control over email operations, while SMTP remains a practical option for systems that already support standard mail-server connections. Webhooks add another layer by allowing applications to respond to delivery events and revision their internal records.

By choosing an integration method that fits the application architecture and following sound security and deliverability practices, developers can build email functionality that supports both immediate communication needs and long-term application growth.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI has taken over everything in the past few years, with AI features bombarding virtually every app or service available. If you’ve ever wanted to just turn off AI features, Canva proves that it could be a simple toggle, if companies actually wanted to give you a choice.

Canva today revealed “AI Controls,” a latest toggle that completely turns off generative AI features within the editing app.

Sources indicate that generative AI can be quite helpful in working on posters, editing images, and more, but it’s not everyone’s preference. Canva puts this well:.

For some people, AI is the most exciting creative tool in a generation, while others prefer bringing their ideas to life without it. We believe the future of creativity should give everyone the freedom to choose their own path, whether that’s creating with AI, without it, or somewhere in between.

To give its users the choice, Canva’s Permissions menu now has a simple toggle for “Enable Generative AI features.” Toggling it off disables features such as Magic Write and Magic Edit. There’s also an option to limit how much AI-generated imagery appears in the Canva library.

Put simply, this is great to see.

AI has its place, but everyone should have a choice like this, especially when it comes to apps and services used for artistry in the same vein as Canva. Yet, the tech industry continues to go in the opposite direction, shoving AI into every corner whether it’s actually useful or not. Canva proves, though, that it doesn’t have to be that way.

The game is finally here, and there’s plenty to discuss.

Industry observers note that it’s hard to believe, but Grand Theft Auto VI is now a real thing that we all can play. Thirteen years after GTA V, and eight years since Red Dead Redemption 2, Rockstar is back with its latest sprawling, extravagant open world. There’s a lot to experience — and a lot to talk about.

Perhaps the most impressive thing about GTA VI is how flexible it is, letting you mold the experience to your own play style. You can still be a maniacal criminal, but you can also focus on the new love story that includes an entire button dedicated to holding hands. Or you can spend the hours fishing or driving around listening to the radio. Maybe you just want to doomscroll through a fake version of Instagram. As GTA VI producer Rob Nelson told me just ahead of launch, “It’s a risk. It’s a real change for Grand Theft Auto. You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.”.

It has been revealed that now that the game is out and people are finding their own way through Leonida, it’s a great time to start talking about it. I’ve played through the entire main story — you can read my review right here — but I’m nowhere close to experiencing everything in the game. But I’m happy to answer any questions you have, though I’ll be careful around some of the big story spoilers. I’ll also be joined by senior reporter Jay Peters, who is still early in the game and can offer a different perspective. There’s a good chance some other Verge staff will stop by as well, since we’re basically all playing it.

According to recent reports, so drop all of your questions, theories, and stray thoughts about GTA VI here. I’ll be checking in throughout the day to join the conversation in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

Industry observers note that for Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other key parts of your digital life — organized.

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

Unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

Proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

Industry observers note that an alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

If that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

It’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

Sources indicate that proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

When you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

Sources indicate that pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

In a recent development, proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that first up, our resident CPU boffin, Jake Roach, has been on the show floor all week, offering us a direct line to all the goings-on at the conference, including an interesting back-and-forth from Nvidia and AMD on their CPUs. AMD claims that its latest EPYC Venice lineup is the best at agentic workloads, while Nvidia's marketing material characterized Nvidia's Vera CPU as being purpose-built for Agentic AI. At SC26, Nvidia CPU chief Ian Finder rebuked Nvidia's own marketing material, stating that the idea that Nvidia could have predicted the Data Center moment was "absurd," instead saying that the firm's design know-how helped them develop the processor.

In this interview, we sit down with Finder to find out how Vera came to be, what agentic workloads mean for the CPU industry, and where Nvidia's headed next.

According to recent reports, nvidia's Vera CPU was a hot topic at SC26, as the manufacturer explained that existing software cannot always take full advantage of the processor without architecture-specific optimization. The company indicated that under some workloads, Vera's performance can be optimized by up to 39% when taking its Olympus-based Arm cores into account. However, it remains to be seen how much performance can be gained from Olympus-specific hardware optimization workloads other than matrix multiplication.

It has been revealed that nvidia also unveiled a Rubin GPU variant, named Rubin HPC, a chip that the company claims is purpose-built for agentic workflows and scientific simulations that demand processing large datasets. While technical details remain scant, Nvidia says that Rubin HPC sports over 50,000 CUDA cores, or slightly below double the number of cores present in the standard-issue Rubin GPU. We explored all the details and possibilities that the newly announced chip might offer.

AMD is now featured in over 40% of the new TOP500 list of supercomputers, with a 14% boost to the tech giant's position. Leading the company is Lux, a supercomputer developed in conjunction with the U.S. Department of Energy. The second supercomputer, Discovery, is expected to debut in 2028, sporting a suite of EPYC CPUs and Instinct accelerators.

Within the TOP500, not much has changed... at the top, with the top 10 systems remaining unchanged, as China's LineShine system in Shenzhen remains at the top of the list, with El Capitan remaining second. We take a look at the entire list and how the focus has seemingly shifted toward AI compute capacity. While the demand for HPC hardware is at an all-time high, it appears as though the vast majority of that hardware isn't being tested against the TOP500 benchmark.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Despite AI clusters seemingly eating up compute capacity, AMD recognizes that the burgeoning segment will never wholly replace HPC computing, and that high-precision workloads will continue to be necessary. AMD's Scott Tease further suggested that building a heterogeneous compute stack would be the best path forward for tackling complex research problems. This point dovetails nicely into how AMD additionally touted that its MI430X's native FP64 operations will beat out emulated support for the full-precision data types seen in Nvidia's hardware. This is notable, as the company claims that Ozaki FP64 emulation could have cascading effects on memory usage, which is in notorious levels of undersupply.

Not wanting to be left out of the conversation, Intel's next-generation Diamond Rapids CPUs surfaced at SC26, but not from Intel itself, curiously. On the ground, we saw the chips turn up at the CXL booth and at Bull, where the CPU was shown installed in a server. While there were no demos available, the tech giant did show off demos for Xeon 6+ and its Crescent Island GPU.

Elsewhere at the show, PCI 6 devices and controllers have started to surface. First, Silicon Motion's SM8466 controller was demoed at the show, armed with PerformaShape 2, which increases the number of quality-of-service sets from 256 to 512, alongside additional boons.

In a recent development, elsewhere, Phison detailed two new enterprise SSDs: one that comes with a built-in NPU and 64GB of memory, and another that is set to merge pSLC cache, with high QLC capacity on a single controller. We explore what makes these devices notable and why, though the company itself notes that the devices are very much still in development.

VAST Data explained how petabyte-scale SSDs will outgrow the tried and true RAID parallel filesystems, according to a simulation the organization ran on its own 900 PB system, which puts the odds of data loss at a staggering 1 in 11 over a decade. We explain all in detail about how it works.

As enterprise hardware and the titanic growth of AI superclusters push the limits of our existing material infrastructure, from interconnects to grid energy and raw materials, researchers from The Ohio State University discussed how high-performance networking could soon scale across entire regions. We explore how faster networking connections could spell a future where distributed computing systems communicate across vast distances.

Industry observers note that while we have a few more articles waiting to be published from SC26, we've also been hard at work publishing stories from other corners of the industry. To read these, you'll need to first arm yourself with a Tom's Hardware Premium subscription.

This week, Anthropic debuted on the NYSE, but the frontier AI lab's debut is also colored by the backdrop of what seems like an endless barrage of fresh vulnerabilities, hacks, and AI-powered action by would-be malfeasants. The conversation around AI safety, sparked by OpenAI's HuggingFace incident, is also being used as a Trojan horse for safety legislation, and against this backdrop, we explore how the companies shaping AI safety might also be the ones warning against using competitors, like capable Chinese open-weight AI models.

Anthropic has also been busy bringing up more compute resources, notably publishing how it managed to get its Claude Mythos model to optimize its software stack to work with AMD Instinct hardware in around three days, with little human oversight. What once was a relentless task that took significant man-hours, an AI can now help complete in mere days. Such a feat could endanger Nvidia's highly lucrative CUDA moat, as AI continues to transform the hardware landscape.

Intel's acquisition of Quantum computing organization Classiq is expected to be completed in the first half of 2027, and following it, Intel is poised to have a chance at becoming the first full-stack quantum computing vendor. The company also plans to manufacture quantum processors on its 18A process, offer foundry services, and eventually sell quantum computers.

Recent findings suggest that an unmanned chip fab might be an unthinkable future today, but it's a future that chipmakers are already planning for. SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron, known rivals in the memory industry, have formed a body to standardize robotic charging, with the aim of having robots from different manufacturers share equipment and therefore cut the costs and complexity of deploying fleets of robotic workers.
